# Plan: triage agent, SPE round r01

Two defaults first. You will place the 40 tickets with their reference labels at `spe/evals/data/tickets.jsonl`. I will build the agent in Python with the Anthropic SDK. I commit locally after each step below. I never push.

## 1. Specify

Spec prompt (verbatim): "triage tickets correctly and cheaply."
Proposals from last round: none, because this is r01.

### Requirements (`spe/spec/spec.md`, round r01)

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Assign exactly one category: billing, bug, how-to, account, or outage | Project definition | Schema check, then exact match to the reference label |
| R2 | Assign exactly one priority from P1 to P4 | Project definition | Schema check, then exact match and within-one match |
| R3 | Draft a first reply that addresses the customer's actual issue | Project definition | Reply judge, rubric item 1 |
| R4 | "Correctly" means category accuracy of at least 0.85 | User's words "correctly", target set by default D1 | Category accuracy |
| R5 | No missed P1 tickets in the eval set | Default D2 | P1 recall equals 1.00 |
| R6 | "Cheaply" means a mean cost of at most $0.010 per ticket | User's words "cheaply", ceiling set by default D3 | Cost per ticket from API usage tokens |
| R7 | The reply promises no refund, credit, ETA, or fix date, and states no facts the ticket does not support | Default D4 | Reply judge, rubric item 2 |
| R8 | Output is valid JSON with fields `category`, `priority`, `reply` | Decision for gradeability | Code schema check |
| R9 | The agent sees only the ticket subject and body. It never sees labels, graders, or predictions | SPE rule | Transcript leak scan |
| R10 | Ticket data stays local and out of git | Default D5 | `git check-ignore spe/evals/data/` passes |

### Open decisions (`spe/spec/disagreements.md`)

| ID | Decision | Owner | Default used in r01 |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Category accuracy target | You | 0.85 |
| D2 | P1 recall target | Support lead | 1.00. A missed outage costs more than a false alarm |
| D3 | Cost ceiling per ticket | You | $0.010 |
| D4 | Reply policy on commitments | Support lead | The reply makes no commitments. It hands off to a human for refunds and ETAs |
| D5 | Ticket data in git | You | The data is gitignored because tickets may hold customer details. I commit a SHA-256 of the file so we can detect changes |
| D6 | Category and priority definitions | Support lead | I write one-line definitions from the category names. I do not read the 40 eval tickets while I write the prompt |
| D7 | Model IDs | You | I use the current Sonnet for C0 and C1 and the current Haiku for C2. I pin the exact IDs after I check the current model docs |
| D8 | One labeler for references | Support lead | I treat the labels as truth. Close-out lists any ticket where all three configs disagree with the label, for the lead to review |
| D9 | Control regrade gate | Process | r01 has no prior round, so I skip the control regrade and log the skip here |
| D10 | Which config wins | You | The cheapest config that meets R4, R5, and R7. If none meets all three, I report that and pick none |

## 2. Predict

### Configurations (each changes one thing from C0)

| Config | Model | Prompt | Changed from C0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| C0 | Sonnet (pinned) | System prompt with definitions, zero-shot | Reference |
| C1 | Sonnet (pinned) | C0 prompt plus 5 synthetic examples I write from the definitions | Adds few-shot examples |
| C2 | Haiku (pinned) | C0 prompt | Model only |

Each metric is the mean over 120 trials per config (40 tickets, 3 trials each). A hit means the measured value falls inside the band. One ticket is 0.025 of accuracy, so the bands are wide on purpose.

### Prediction table

| Metric | C0 | C1 | C2 | Grader check | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Category accuracy | 0.85 ± 0.07 | 0.88 ± 0.07 | 0.80 ± 0.08 | Code: exact match to `ref_category` | Most tickets name their topic. The errors will fall on bug versus outage and billing versus account. Examples help on those edges, and Haiku is weaker on them |
| Priority exact accuracy | 0.60 ± 0.10 | 0.65 ± 0.10 | 0.55 ± 0.10 | Code: exact match to `ref_priority` | The lead's priority rules are unwritten, so the model must guess the line between P2 and P3 |
| Priority within one level | 0.92 ± 0.05 | 0.93 ± 0.05 | 0.90 ± 0.06 | Code: absolute difference of at most 1 | The model will rarely be far off even when it misses the exact level |
| P1 recall | 0.85 ± 0.15 | 0.90 ± 0.10 | 0.80 ± 0.20 | Code: share of trials on reference-P1 tickets that output P1 | Outage language is loud. The set likely holds only 3 to 6 P1 tickets, so one miss moves the number a lot |
| Reply pass rate | 0.85 ± 0.08 | 0.85 ± 0.08 | 0.75 ± 0.10 | Judge: rubric item 1 (addresses the issue, correct tone, asks for missing info) | Sonnet writes a good first reply without examples. Haiku replies are thinner on how-to tickets |
| Unsafe reply rate | 0.05 ± 0.05 | 0.04 ± 0.04 | 0.08 ± 0.06 | Judge: rubric item 2 (commitment or invented fact) | The prompt forbids commitments, but billing tickets pull the model toward offering refunds |
| Schema valid rate | 1.00 ± 0.01 | 1.00 ± 0.01 | 0.99 ± 0.01 | Code: JSON schema validation | Structured output through a tool schema almost never fails |
| Cost per ticket (USD) | 0.011 ± 0.004 | 0.018 ± 0.006 | 0.004 ± 0.002 | Code: usage tokens times the price table in `triage/prices.py` | About 1,500 input and 400 output tokens per ticket. The examples add about 2,500 input tokens to C1. Haiku costs about a third as much per token |

Same as last round: not applicable in r01. The naive guess at close-out is "C1 and C2 score the same as C0". I will say plainly if that guess beats these predictions.

Expected outcome: C2 is the only config under the R6 cost ceiling, and it is likely to miss R4. C0 sits on the cost ceiling. If this holds, D10 picks no winner, and r02 tests cheaper prompts on Sonnet or a better prompt on Haiku.

## 3. Evaluate

### Steps, gates, and commits

| Step | Work | Gate to pass | Local commit |

| 1 | Create `spe/`. Save the transcript to `spe/spec/transcripts/2026-10-21-r01.md` verbatim. Write `spec.md` and `disagreements.md`. Copy this plan to `spe/plans/r01.md`. Write `spe/predictions/r01.yaml`. Add `spe/evals/data/` to `.gitignore` | The prediction file exists before any trial runs | `spe r01: spec, plan, and prediction` |
| 2 | Build the agent: `triage/agent.py`, `triage/run.py`, `triage/schema.json`, `triage/prices.py`, `triage/prompts/system.md`, `triage/prompts/fewshot.md` | One synthetic ticket returns valid JSON on each config | `triage: first agent with configs C0, C1, C2` |
| 3 | Split `tickets.jsonl` into `tickets_input.jsonl` (id, subject, body) and `labels.jsonl`. Build graders in `spe/evals/harness/graders/` (`code_checks.py`, `judge_reply.md`, `selftest.py`) and `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js` | File hash recorded. Labels file is not in any agent path | `spe r01: graders and workflow harness` |
| 4 | Gate G1, grader selftest | Oracle output (the labels themselves) scores 1.00 on category and priority. Empty output and shifted labels score 0. The judge passes a hand-written good reply and fails an empty reply and a reply written for a different ticket | `spe r01: gates passed` (one commit after G3) |
| 5 | Gate G2, control regrade | Skipped in r01 under D9 | Same commit |
| 6 | Gate G3, dry run on 3 cells: one ticket each on C0, C1, C2 | Schema valid, cost logged, leak scan clean, judge returns a verdict | Same commit |
| 7 | Launch the Workflow. It returns at launch | None | None until it completes |
| 8 | Close-out when the completion notice arrives (see below) | Every prediction scored | `spe r01: learn`, then tag `spe-r01` |

The prediction file starts with `# Saved before the eval ran. Do not edit after the run.` It holds round, date, author ("Claude, approved by the user in plan mode"), configs, each number with its band and Why, and `same_as_last_round: null`.

### Workflow arguments (`r01-workflow.js`)

```js
const ROUND = "r01";
const ARGS = {
  configs: ["C0", "C1", "C2"],
  tickets: "spe/evals/data/tickets_input.jsonl",  // 40 tickets
  trials_per_cell: 3,                              // 120 cells, 360 trials
  split_cell_rule: "trials disagree on category or priority",
  split_extra_trials: 2,                           // per split cell
  split_cell_cap: 20,
  judge_model: "Opus (pinned)",                    // blind to config, not the agent's model
  budget_usd: 25,                                  // skip and log any trial that would cross it
  concurrency: 6,
  forbidden_paths: [
    "spe/evals/data/labels.jsonl",
    "spe/evals/harness/graders/",
    "spe/predictions/"
  ]
};
```

Workflow phases: run trials, run code checks, run the judge only on the reply, scan transcripts and void any trial that touched a forbidden path, top up split cells, run failure analysis, then run a completeness critic that checks every cell has a graded result or a logged skip.

### Cost estimate (unmeasured)

These prices are estimates. I will check them against current pricing before the run.

| Item | Trials | Est. per trial | Est. total |
|---|---|---|---|
| C0 agent | 120 | $0.011 | $1.30 |
| C1 agent | 120 | $0.018 | $2.20 |
| C2 agent | 120 | $0.004 | $0.50 |
| Reply judge | 360 | $0.018 | $6.30 |
| Split-cell top-ups | up to 40 | about $0.03 | $1.20 |
| Total | | | about $11.50 |

The cap is $25. The Claude Code session tokens that drive the Workflow are not in this figure.

### Halt conditions

I halt and report to you if any of these happen: spend reaches the $25 cap, a trial reads a forbidden path, a gate fails, or a result needs one of the open decisions above. If every config scores the maximum on a metric, I mark that prediction as not scorable, check once for a leak or grader bug, and ask you whether to use harder tickets or stricter graders.

### Close-out (step 8)

- `spe/prediction-log.md`: Metric, Config, Predicted, Measured, Same as last round, Verdict, Closer. Under it, "Which Why broke" quotes each missed Why and names the wrong assumption.
- `spe/failures.md`: each new failure type as F1, F2, and so on, with name, kind, round, What, How to spot it, Seen in, and Fix.
- A "Proposed for round r02" table in `spec.md`, plus `spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml` marked `status: draft`.
- The list of tickets where all configs disagree with the label, for the support lead (D8).
- `spe/README.md` updated with the r01 headline and the winning config, or a note that no config won.
critiques: The plan quotes the spec prompt verbatim and turns "correctly" and "cheaply" into R4 (category accuracy at least 0.85) and R6 (mean cost at most $0.010). The requirements table gives every row, R1 through R10, a Test column with a concrete check.

The prediction table gives C0, C1, and C2 a number with a band for each of 8 metrics. Examples are category accuracy of 0.85 ± 0.07 and cost of 0.011 ± 0.004 USD. The table uses no adjectives in place of numbers.

Each metric row has a Why that explains its numbers. For example, the cost Why cites about 1,500 input and 400 output tokens, about 2,500 extra input tokens for C1, and Haiku at about a third of the price.

Step 1 copies the plan to spe/plans/r01.md and writes spe/predictions/r01.yaml. It commits them as "spe r01: spec, plan, and prediction" under the gate "The prediction file exists before any trial runs".

The eval runs as a Workflow (r01-workflow.js) that launches in step 7. Before that, Gate G1 runs a grader selftest with oracle, empty, and shifted labels plus judge cases. Gate G3 runs a 3-cell dry run.

The prediction table has a Grader check column that names the grader for each metric. Examples are "Code: exact match to ref_category" and "Judge: rubric item 2", and cost comes from usage tokens times the price table in triage/prices.py.

Step 8 writes spe/prediction-log.md with Predicted, Measured, and Verdict columns, plus a "Which Why broke" section. It seeds round r02 with a "Proposed for round r02" table and spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml.
